questions.title: Build a home loan amortisation schedule
questions.scenario: Rohan Mehta in the retail loans team gets daily calls from home loan customers asking how much of each EMI goes to interest. He wants the full month-by-month schedule generated in SQL instead of a spreadsheet, with the last EMI adjusted so the balance closes at exactly zero.
questions.schema:
LOAN(loan_id NUMBER, principal NUMBER(14,2), annual_rate NUMBER(5,2), tenure_months NUMBER, emi NUMBER(12,2), first_due DATE)
-- annual_rate like 8.75 (percent per year); emi is the fixed monthly instalment in INR
-- first_due is the first EMI date, no time part
questions.task: For one loan (:loan_id) list month_no, due_date, opening balance, interest, principal part, closing balance and amount due, ending with a zero closing balance.
questions.hint: Use recursive subquery factoring that carries the opening balance forward one month at a time, and compute due dates from first_due, not from the previous due date.
questions.solution:
WITH sched (loan_id, month_no, due_date, opening, annual_rate, emi, tenure_months, first_due) AS (
  SELECT loan_id, 1, first_due, principal, annual_rate, emi, tenure_months, first_due
  FROM   loan
  WHERE  loan_id = :loan_id
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.loan_id, s.month_no + 1,
         ADD_MONTHS(s.first_due, s.month_no),
         s.opening - (s.emi - ROUND(s.opening * s.annual_rate / 1200, 2)),
         s.annual_rate, s.emi, s.tenure_months, s.first_due
  FROM   sched s
  WHERE  s.month_no < s.tenure_months
)
SELECT month_no, due_date, opening,
       ROUND(opening * annual_rate / 1200, 2) AS interest,
       CASE WHEN month_no = tenure_months THEN opening
            ELSE emi - ROUND(opening * annual_rate / 1200, 2) END AS principal_part,
       CASE WHEN month_no = tenure_months THEN 0
            ELSE opening - (emi - ROUND(opening * annual_rate / 1200, 2)) END AS closing,
       CASE WHEN month_no = tenure_months
            THEN opening + ROUND(opening * annual_rate / 1200, 2)
            ELSE emi END AS amount_due
FROM   sched
ORDER  BY month_no;
questions.why: The anchor row is month 1 with the full principal; each recursive step subtracts that month's principal part (EMI minus interest at rate/1200) to get the next opening balance. The last month pays whatever is left plus its interest, so rounding differences do not leave a few rupees outstanding. Due dates use ADD_MONTHS from first_due so a 31st does not drift to the 28th forever after February.
questions.tip: Recursive WITH needs a column list, an anchor, a recursive member that references the CTE once, and a stop condition; I keep the stop condition on a counter so it can never loop.
questions.simple: A loan schedule is like a staircase. Each month you start with what you owe, pay some interest and some of the loan, and what is left becomes next month's starting point. A recursive WITH builds one step, then uses it to build the next step, until the loan is paid off.
questions.remember: Recursive WITH = build the next row from the row before.

questions.title: Sector-wise GNPA for regulatory return
questions.scenario: Ananya Iyer prepares the quarterly sector-wise advances return for RBI. She needs outstanding and gross NPA by region and sector, sector totals across all regions, and a grand total, but the format has no region subtotal rows. Some legacy loans have no sector and must show as 'Unclassified', not be confused with a total row.
questions.schema:
ADVANCES(loan_id NUMBER, region VARCHAR2(20), sector VARCHAR2(30), npa_flag CHAR(1), outstanding NUMBER(16,2), asof_date DATE)
-- sector like 'Agriculture','MSME','Retail' or NULL for legacy loans
-- npa_flag 'Y' or 'N'; asof_date is the snapshot date with no time part
questions.task: For the 31-Mar-2026 snapshot return row_type, region, sector, total outstanding, NPA outstanding and GNPA % for (region, sector), (sector) and grand total only.
questions.hint: GROUPING SETS lets you list exactly the groupings you want, and GROUPING() tells a real NULL apart from a subtotal NULL.
questions.solution:
SELECT CASE GROUPING_ID(region, sector)
         WHEN 0 THEN 'Region x Sector'
         WHEN 2 THEN 'Sector total'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'Grand total'
       END AS row_type,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE NVL(region, 'Unknown') END AS region,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(sector) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE NVL(sector, 'Unclassified') END AS sector,
       SUM(outstanding) AS total_os,
       SUM(CASE WHEN npa_flag = 'Y' THEN outstanding ELSE 0 END) AS npa_os,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(CASE WHEN npa_flag = 'Y' THEN outstanding ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(outstanding), 0), 2) AS gnpa_pct
FROM   advances
WHERE  asof_date = DATE '2026-03-31'
GROUP  BY GROUPING SETS ((region, sector), (sector), ())
ORDER  BY GROUPING_ID(region, sector), sector, region;
questions.why: ROLLUP(region, sector) would produce region subtotals and no sector totals, so GROUPING SETS is the precise tool. GROUPING_ID builds a bit pattern (region = 2, sector = 1), giving 0 for detail, 2 for sector totals and 3 for the grand total. Checking GROUPING() before NVL means a legacy loan with NULL sector shows 'Unclassified' while the subtotal row shows 'ALL'.
questions.tip: ROLLUP and CUBE are shortcuts for fixed sets of groupings; when a report format needs a specific mix I write GROUPING SETS and label rows with GROUPING_ID.
questions.simple: The report needs some lines by sector and region, some totals by sector, and one grand total, but not every possible mix. GROUPING SETS lets you list exactly which totals you want, like picking only the dishes you want from a menu instead of the full buffet.
questions.remember: GROUPING SETS = choose exactly which totals you want.

questions.title: Optional-filter AML alert search
questions.scenario: Vikram Rao's AML operations screen lets analysts filter open alerts by branch, minimum amount and from-date, any of which can be blank. The current code concatenates the typed values into the SQL string, which the information security audit flagged as SQL injection risk, and the DBA says it floods the shared pool with one-off statements.
questions.schema:
AML_ALERT(alert_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, branch_code VARCHAR2(10), alert_amt NUMBER(14,2), alert_dt DATE, status VARCHAR2(10))
-- status 'OPEN' or 'CLOSED'; alert_amt in INR
questions.task: Write a function get_alerts(p_branch, p_min_amt, p_from_dt) that returns a SYS_REFCURSOR of open alerts, applying only the filters that are not NULL, using bind variables only.
questions.hint: Keep the number of binds fixed by adding a harmless '(1 = 1 OR :x IS NULL)' when a filter is not supplied, then OPEN ... FOR ... USING.
questions.why: User values never become part of the SQL text, they are passed through USING, so nothing typed can change the statement and injection is impossible. There are at most 8 distinct SQL texts, so Oracle parses each once and reuses its plan instead of hard-parsing (building a fresh plan, which is CPU-heavy) for every search. Each text only has the predicates that apply, so the optimizer can use an index on branch_code when that filter is given.
questions.tip: With dynamic SQL I bind values and only concatenate structure I control; the '1 = 1 OR :x IS NULL' trick keeps the USING list fixed while each filter combination still gets its own good plan.
questions.simple: A search screen where the user fills only some boxes. You build the SQL with only the filters they filled. But you never paste what they typed into the SQL; you pass it separately, like putting a letter in an envelope instead of writing on the outside. That keeps it safe from hackers and fast.
questions.remember: Build the shape, pass the values separately with binds.
questions.output_note: Rows returned by get_alerts('PUN01', NULL, NULL). Alert 3 is also PUN01 but CLOSED.

questions.title: Carry forward USD/INR on holidays
questions.scenario: Sneha Kulkarni in treasury revalues foreign currency positions every calendar day, but reference rates are only published on business days. For weekends and holidays she must use the last published rate, and 1-Nov-2026 is a Sunday so it needs the last October rate.
questions.schema:
FX_RATE(rate_date DATE, ccy CHAR(3), rate NUMBER(10,4))
-- one row per business day per currency, no time part
-- rate = INR per 1 unit of ccy
questions.task: Return every calendar day of November 2026 with the USD/INR rate to use and whether it was published that day or carried forward.
questions.hint: Generate a calendar, outer join the rates, include some October rows for the lookback, and use LAST_VALUE(... IGNORE NULLS).
questions.solution:
WITH cal AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-01' + LEVEL - 1 AS d
  FROM   dual
  CONNECT BY LEVEL <= DATE '2026-12-01' - DATE '2026-11-01'
),
src AS (
  SELECT rate_date, rate
  FROM   fx_rate
  WHERE  ccy = 'USD'
  AND    rate_date >= DATE '2026-10-01'
  AND    rate_date <  DATE '2026-12-01'
),
all_days AS (
  SELECT c.d, s.rate
  FROM   cal c LEFT JOIN src s ON s.rate_date = c.d
  UNION ALL
  SELECT rate_date, rate FROM src WHERE rate_date < DATE '2026-11-01'
)
SELECT rate_date, usd_inr, rate_src
FROM (
  SELECT d AS rate_date,
         LAST_VALUE(rate IGNORE NULLS)
           OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS usd_inr,
         CASE WHEN rate IS NULL THEN 'Carried' ELSE 'Published' END AS rate_src
  FROM   all_days
)
WHERE  rate_date >= DATE '2026-11-01'
ORDER  BY rate_date;
questions.why: The calendar guarantees one row per day, and the outer join leaves rate NULL on non-business days. LAST_VALUE with IGNORE NULLS over all rows up to the current one picks the most recent non-NULL rate, and the October rows are only there so 1-Nov has something to look back to. The filter to November is applied outside the window, otherwise the October rows would be removed before the analytic function sees them.
questions.tip: For carry-forward I use LAST_VALUE IGNORE NULLS with an explicit ROWS frame, and I filter after the window so the lookback rows are still visible to it.
questions.simple: On holidays there is no new exchange rate, so you use the last one you had, like a scoreboard that keeps showing the last score until a new goal is scored. LAST_VALUE IGNORE NULLS looks back and picks the most recent rate that is not empty.
questions.remember: IGNORE NULLS = carry the last known value forward.

questions.title: Card EMI due dates in March
questions.scenario: Kavya Nair in credit card operations found that customers who converted a 30-Jan purchase into EMI were billed on 31-Mar, because the old job did ADD_MONTHS on the previous due date. The rule is: due on the same day number as the purchase, or the month's last day if that day does not exist. Purchase timestamps include the time of swipe.
questions.schema:
CARD_EMI(emi_plan_id NUMBER, card_ref VARCHAR2(20), purchase_dt DATE, amount NUMBER(12,2), tenure_months NUMBER, emi_amt NUMBER(12,2))
-- purchase_dt has a time part, e.g. 30-Jan-2026 21:14
-- instalment n is due n months after purchase; tenure up to 60
questions.task: List emi_plan_id, instalment number, due date and EMI amount for every instalment falling due in March 2026.
questions.hint: ADD_MONTHS jumps to the last day of the target month when the start date is a month end (28-Feb becomes 31-Mar), so build the date from the first of the month plus the day number and cap it with LAST_DAY.
questions.solution:
WITH n AS (
  SELECT LEVEL AS inst_no FROM dual CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 60
)
SELECT emi_plan_id, inst_no, due_date, emi_amt
FROM (
  SELECT e.emi_plan_id, n.inst_no, e.emi_amt,
         LEAST(ADD_MONTHS(TRUNC(e.purchase_dt, 'MM'), n.inst_no)
                 + EXTRACT(DAY FROM e.purchase_dt) - 1,
               LAST_DAY(ADD_MONTHS(TRUNC(e.purchase_dt, 'MM'), n.inst_no))) AS due_date
  FROM   card_emi e
  JOIN   n ON n.inst_no <= e.tenure_months
)
WHERE  due_date >= DATE '2026-03-01'
AND    due_date <  DATE '2026-04-01'
ORDER  BY due_date, emi_plan_id;
questions.why: Chaining ADD_MONTHS loses the original day (30-Jan to 28-Feb to 31-Mar), and even a single ADD_MONTHS turns 28-Feb into 31-Mar because of Oracle's last-day rule. Starting from the first of the month, adding the day number minus one and capping with LAST_DAY gives 28-Feb, 30-Mar and 28-Mar exactly as the rule says. TRUNC removes the swipe time and the half-open range from 1-Mar to before 1-Apr catches the whole of 31-Mar.
questions.tip: I always compute instalment dates from the original start date, never the previous due date, and I remember ADD_MONTHS maps a month-end to a month-end.
questions.simple: A due date on the 30th is tricky because February has only 28 days. Start from the 1st of the month, move to the right day, and if the month is shorter, stop at its last day. Always count from the original date, not from last month's date, or the day keeps slipping.
questions.remember: Start from the 1st, add the day, cap at the month's last day.

questions.title: UPI payments from unrecognised devices
questions.scenario: Arjun Malhotra on the fraud desk wants yesterday's high-value UPI payments made from a device other than the customer's bound device. His first query used t.device_id <> d.reg_device_id and missed the riskiest cases: payments where the app failed to capture the device and customers who never bound one.
questions.schema:
UPI_TXN(txn_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, device_id VARCHAR2(64), amount NUMBER(12,2), txn_ts DATE)
-- device_id NULL when the SDK failed to capture it; txn_ts has a time part
CUSTOMER_DEVICE(cust_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, reg_device_id VARCHAR2(64))
-- reg_device_id NULL, or no row at all, if the customer never bound a device
questions.task: List UPI payments of INR 10,000 or more on 11-Nov-2026 where the device does not match the bound device, treating a NULL or missing value on either side as a mismatch.
questions.hint: A comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so use an outer join and LNNVL (or explicit IS NULL checks) to keep those rows.
questions.solution:
SELECT t.txn_id, t.cust_id, t.amount, t.txn_ts,
       t.device_id, d.reg_device_id
FROM   upi_txn t
LEFT   JOIN customer_device d ON d.cust_id = t.cust_id
WHERE  t.txn_ts >= DATE '2026-11-11'
AND    t.txn_ts <  DATE '2026-11-12'
AND    t.amount >= 10000
AND    LNNVL(t.device_id = d.reg_device_id)
ORDER  BY t.amount DESC;
questions.why: t.device_id <> d.reg_device_id is UNKNOWN when either side is NULL, and WHERE drops UNKNOWN rows, so the riskiest payments vanished. LNNVL(condition) returns TRUE when the condition is FALSE or UNKNOWN, which is exactly 'not a confirmed match'; the LEFT JOIN keeps customers with no CUSTOMER_DEVICE row. The equivalent long form is t.device_id IS NULL OR d.reg_device_id IS NULL OR t.device_id <> d.reg_device_id.
questions.tip: Whenever I write <> on nullable columns I ask what NULL should mean, and for 'not a confirmed match' I use LNNVL or explicit IS NULL checks.
questions.simple: If you do not know which phone a person registered, you cannot say the payment came from the right phone. Oracle treats 'not equal' with an unknown value as 'I don't know' and hides those rows. LNNVL says 'show me anything that is not a sure match', so the risky unknown ones stay in the list.
questions.remember: Unknown is not a match; LNNVL keeps the unknowns.

questions.title: List all NRE accounts
questions.scenario: Shalini Rao in the NRI desk must send a balance list of all NRE (Non-Resident External) accounts to the relationship managers before the month-end call. In this bank every NRE account number starts with the letters NRE.
questions.schema:
ACCOUNT(acct_no VARCHAR2(14), cust_name VARCHAR2(60), acct_type VARCHAR2(10), balance NUMBER(14,2))
-- acct_no prefix tells the product: NRE..., NRO..., SB..., CA...
-- balance in INR
questions.task: List acct_no, cust_name and balance of every account whose number starts with NRE, biggest balance first.
questions.hint: Use LIKE with the % wildcard after the fixed letters, so only the start of the number is checked.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_no, cust_name, balance
FROM   account
WHERE  acct_no LIKE 'NRE%'
ORDER  BY balance DESC;
questions.simple: Think of a school register where you want every name that starts with 'Ra'. You only look at the first letters and do not care what comes after. LIKE 'NRE%' does the same: the % means 'anything can come after this'. So CA4001NRE is not picked, because NRE is at the end, not the start.
questions.remember: % = anything after; 'NRE%' means starts with NRE.
questions.why: LIKE compares a string to a pattern where % matches zero or more characters and _ matches exactly one. With the wildcard only at the end ('NRE%'), Oracle can still use an index on acct_no as a range scan, whereas a leading wildcard ('%NRE') forces it to check every row. The match is case-sensitive, so 'nre1004' would not be returned.
questions.tip: I keep the wildcard at the end of a LIKE pattern when I can, because 'ABC%' can use an index and '%ABC' cannot.

questions.title: SIPs bigger than the average
questions.scenario: Karthik Menon, who runs the SIP desk at an AMC, wants to call investors whose monthly SIP is above the average SIP amount and offer them a premium advisory service. He needs the list from the SIP register.
questions.schema:
SIP(sip_id NUMBER, investor_name VARCHAR2(60), scheme VARCHAR2(40), monthly_amount NUMBER(10,2))
-- monthly_amount is the SIP instalment in INR
questions.task: List sip_id, investor_name and monthly_amount for SIPs whose monthly_amount is greater than the average monthly_amount of all SIPs, biggest first.
questions.hint: Put SELECT AVG(monthly_amount) FROM sip in brackets inside the WHERE clause.
questions.solution:
SELECT sip_id, investor_name, monthly_amount
FROM   sip
WHERE  monthly_amount > (SELECT AVG(monthly_amount) FROM sip)
ORDER  BY monthly_amount DESC;
questions.simple: Imagine your class gets marks and the teacher first works out the class average. Then she reads out only the names who scored more than that average. The query in brackets works out the average first, and the outer query keeps only the rows above it. Here the average is 6000, so only the 10000 and 15000 SIPs are shown.
questions.remember: Inner query finds the average; outer query compares with it.
questions.why: A scalar subquery returns exactly one value, so it can be used anywhere a single number is allowed, such as the right side of >. Oracle evaluates it once because it does not refer to the outer row. You cannot write WHERE monthly_amount > AVG(monthly_amount) directly, because aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE.
questions.tip: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE, so to compare each row with an overall average I use a scalar subquery or AVG() OVER ().

questions.title: Split cardholders into four spend bands
questions.scenario: Priya Deshpande in credit card marketing wants to divide cardholders into four equal-sized bands by October spend, so band 1 gets a lounge-access offer and band 4 gets a spend-more cashback. Two cardholders spent exactly the same amount and she wants the result repeatable every time it is run.
questions.schema:
CARD_SPEND(card_id NUMBER, holder_name VARCHAR2(60), oct_spend NUMBER(12,2))
-- oct_spend is total October 2026 spend in INR
questions.task: Show card_id, holder_name, oct_spend and spend_band (1 = highest spenders) using four bands, breaking ties by card_id.
questions.hint: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY ...) deals the rows into 4 buckets; add card_id to the ORDER BY so ties always land the same way.
questions.solution:
SELECT card_id, holder_name, oct_spend,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY oct_spend DESC, card_id) AS spend_band
FROM   card_spend
ORDER  BY spend_band, oct_spend DESC, card_id;
questions.simple: Think of a teacher splitting a line of 7 children into 4 teams, tallest first. 7 does not divide by 4, so the first three teams get 2 children and the last team gets 1. NTILE(4) does exactly this with rows. When two children are the same height, the roll number decides who goes first, so the teams are the same every time.
questions.remember: NTILE(n) = deal rows into n teams, extras go to the first teams.
questions.why: NTILE(n) sorts the rows and assigns bucket numbers so bucket sizes differ by at most one, with the larger buckets first (7 rows into 4 gives 2,2,2,1). It is based on row position, not value, so tied amounts can fall into different buckets; adding a unique tiebreaker like card_id makes the assignment deterministic. If you need equal-value rows to stay together, use a value-based rule such as WIDTH_BUCKET or PERCENT_RANK instead.
questions.tip: NTILE splits by row count not by value, so I always add a unique tiebreaker to its ORDER BY to make the bands reproducible.
questions.output_note: 7 rows into 4 bands gives sizes 2, 2, 2, 1. The tie at 96000 is broken by card_id.

questions.title: Each bank's share of daily NEFT
questions.scenario: Rajesh Iyer in payments operations reviews outward NEFT settlement files and wants each remitter bank's percentage share of the day's value, to spot concentration. On 10-11-2026 the ICICI file had not reconciled yet, so its amount is still NULL.
questions.schema:
NEFT_SUMMARY(batch_date DATE, remitter_bank VARCHAR2(20), txn_count NUMBER, amount_inr NUMBER(16,2))
-- one row per bank per day; amount_inr NULL until the file reconciles
questions.task: For every row show batch_date, remitter_bank, amount_inr and share_pct (percentage of that day's total amount, 2 decimals), highest share first within each day.
questions.hint: Use RATIO_TO_REPORT(amount_inr) OVER (PARTITION BY batch_date) and multiply by 100; the NULL row gets a NULL share.
questions.solution:
SELECT batch_date, remitter_bank, amount_inr,
       ROUND(100 * RATIO_TO_REPORT(amount_inr)
                     OVER (PARTITION BY batch_date), 2) AS share_pct
FROM   neft_summary
ORDER  BY batch_date, share_pct DESC NULLS LAST;
questions.simple: Think of a pizza shared by friends each day. Each friend's share is their slices divided by that day's total slices. RATIO_TO_REPORT does this division for every row, and PARTITION BY batch_date makes sure each day is its own pizza. A friend whose slices are unknown (NULL) gets an unknown share, and the others are counted without him.
questions.remember: RATIO_TO_REPORT = my part divided by the group total.
questions.why: RATIO_TO_REPORT(x) OVER (PARTITION BY p) equals x / SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY p), so it avoids a self-join or a second GROUP BY. SUM ignores NULLs, so the day's total is built only from the reconciled banks and the NULL row's own ratio is NULL. Forgetting PARTITION BY would divide by the grand total of all days.
questions.tip: For percent-of-total I use RATIO_TO_REPORT or x / SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY ...) instead of joining back to an aggregated subquery.
questions.output_note: The 10-11-2026 total is 12,00,00,000 because the NULL ICICI amount is ignored.

questions.title: GL versus sub-ledger breaks with collections
questions.scenario: Deepak Narayan in finance control runs the daily GL to sub-ledger reconciliation and wants every break written to RECON_BREAK: amounts that differ, GL codes with no sub-ledger total, and sub-ledger codes missing from the GL. He wants it done in one PL/SQL pass using an associative array keyed by GL code instead of a FULL OUTER JOIN.
questions.schema:
GL_BALANCE(gl_code VARCHAR2(10) PRIMARY KEY, balance NUMBER(16,2))
-- closing balance per GL code in INR
SUBLEDGER_TOTAL(gl_code VARCHAR2(10) PRIMARY KEY, sl_balance NUMBER(16,2))
-- sum of sub-ledger accounts mapped to the GL code
RECON_BREAK(gl_code VARCHAR2(10), gl_bal NUMBER(16,2), sl_bal NUMBER(16,2), diff NUMBER(16,2))
-- diff = NVL(gl_bal,0) - NVL(sl_bal,0); empty before the run
questions.task: Write an anonymous block that loads GL_BALANCE into an associative array indexed by gl_code, walks SUBLEDGER_TOTAL, and inserts every mismatch, sub-ledger-only code and GL-only code into RECON_BREAK.
questions.hint: Delete each matched key from the array as you go; whatever keys remain at the end are GL codes with no sub-ledger, and you can walk them with FIRST and NEXT.
questions.simple: Imagine your teacher has a list of children who should be in class, and you tick each child off as they walk in. Children who walk in but are not on the list are a problem. Names still not ticked at the end are absent. The associative array is that list with names as labels: we tick off (delete) each match, write down the problems, and whatever names are left at the end are the missing ones.
questions.remember: Tick off matches; leftovers in the array are the missing ones.
questions.why: An INDEX BY VARCHAR2 associative array gives keyed lookups in memory, so EXISTS and direct access by gl_code replace a join. Deleting matched keys makes the leftovers exactly the GL-only codes, and FIRST/NEXT walk string keys in sorted order, so the output is deterministic. EXISTS must be checked before reading l_gl(key), because reading a missing key raises NO_DATA_FOUND.
questions.tip: Before reading an associative array element I check .EXISTS, because a missing key raises NO_DATA_FOUND, and I walk sparse arrays with FIRST/NEXT, never a 1..COUNT loop.
questions.output_note: RECON_BREAK after the block, in insert order: 10020 differs by 2500, 40010 exists only in the sub-ledger, 30010 exists only in the GL.

questions.title: Continuous cover periods per member
questions.scenario: Anjali Saxena in health insurance claims checks pre-existing-disease waiting periods, which only count if cover was continuous. A member can have several policies, renewals and top-ups that overlap or start the day after the previous one ends, and she wants each member's unbroken cover blocks.
questions.schema:
POLICY_COVER(member_id NUMBER, policy_no VARCHAR2(20), start_dt DATE, end_dt DATE)
-- one row per policy or top-up; dates inclusive, no time part
-- a policy starting the day after another ends counts as continuous
questions.task: Return member_id, cover_from and cover_to for each continuous block of cover, merging ranges that overlap or touch (next start = previous end + 1).
questions.hint: Compare each start_dt with the largest end_dt seen so far for that member (MAX over the earlier rows); start a new group when the gap is more than one day, then GROUP BY that group.
questions.solution:
WITH s AS (
  SELECT member_id, start_dt, end_dt,
         MAX(end_dt) OVER (PARTITION BY member_id
                           ORDER BY start_dt, end_dt
                           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS prev_max_end
  FROM   policy_cover
), g AS (
  SELECT s.*,
         SUM(CASE WHEN prev_max_end >= start_dt - 1 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY start_dt, end_dt
                 ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS grp
  FROM   s
)
SELECT member_id, MIN(start_dt) AS cover_from, MAX(end_dt) AS cover_to
FROM   g
GROUP  BY member_id, grp
ORDER  BY member_id, cover_from;
questions.simple: Imagine laying paper strips on a ruler, one strip for each policy. Where strips overlap or touch, you tape them into one long strip. Where there is a gap, you start a new strip. The query checks whether each new strip starts before the furthest point covered so far (plus one day). If yes it joins the current strip, if not it starts a new one.
questions.remember: Starts after the furthest end plus one? New block.
questions.why: Comparing with only the previous row's end_dt fails when an earlier long policy covers a later short one, so the running MAX(end_dt) over all earlier rows is used. A running SUM of 'new block' flags turns the rows into group numbers (gaps-and-islands), and MIN/MAX per group gives each block. The frame ending at 1 PRECEDING excludes the current row, and its NULL on the first row correctly starts group 1.
questions.tip: To merge intervals I use a running MAX of end dates, not LAG, because a long earlier interval can swallow several later ones.
questions.output_note: Member 502 has a gap from 01-04-2026 to 14-05-2026, so the waiting period restarts.

questions.title: Catch cash deposits split below 50,000
questions.scenario: Sunita Bhatt in the AML cell knows PAN is mandatory for cash deposits of INR 50,000 or more, so some customers split cash into deposits just under that limit. She wants accounts with three or more back-to-back cash deposits of INR 45,000 to 49,999, all within 7 days of the first one, flagged for an STR review.
questions.schema:
CASH_DEPOSIT(txn_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, txn_ts DATE, amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- cash deposits only; txn_ts has a time part; amount in INR
questions.task: For each run of 3 or more consecutive deposits per account that are each between 45,000 and 49,999 and fall within 7 days (168 hours) of the run's first deposit, show acct_id, first_ts, last_ts, dep_count and total_amt.
questions.hint: Use MATCH_RECOGNIZE with PATTERN (s{3,}) and put both the amount band and txn_ts < FIRST(txn_ts) + 7 inside DEFINE.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id, first_ts, last_ts, dep_count, total_amt
FROM   cash_deposit
MATCH_RECOGNIZE (
  PARTITION BY acct_id
  ORDER BY txn_ts
  MEASURES FIRST(txn_ts) AS first_ts,
           LAST(txn_ts)  AS last_ts,
           COUNT(*)      AS dep_count,
           SUM(amount)   AS total_amt
  ONE ROW PER MATCH
  AFTER MATCH SKIP PAST LAST ROW
  PATTERN (s{3,})
  DEFINE s AS amount BETWEEN 45000 AND 49999
          AND txn_ts < FIRST(txn_ts) + 7
)
ORDER  BY acct_id, first_ts;
questions.simple: Think of a stopwatch that starts at a customer's first 'just under the limit' deposit. Every next deposit just under the limit is counted, as long as the stopwatch shows less than 7 days. A big normal deposit or the stopwatch running out stops the count. If the count reaches 3 or more, the account is flagged.
questions.remember: PATTERN finds the run; DEFINE says what each step must look like.
questions.why: MATCH_RECOGNIZE scans rows in ORDER BY txn_ts per account and greedily extends s{3,} while each row satisfies DEFINE. FIRST(txn_ts) inside DEFINE refers to the first row of the match being built, so the 7-day window is anchored to the start of the run; DATE + 7 adds exactly 168 hours. Account 9003's third deposit is 30 minutes past the 7-day mark and account 9002's run is broken by an INR 1,20,000 deposit, so only 9001 matches.
questions.tip: For 'N events within T of the first' I put FIRST(ts) + T in DEFINE, because MATCH_RECOGNIZE handles the sequence and the time limit in one pass.

questions.title: Match share sales to buy lots FIFO
questions.scenario: Manoj Thakur in the broking back office prepares capital-gains statements, and income-tax rules require shares sold to be matched to the earliest purchases first (FIFO). Clients bought in several lots, two of them on the same day, and he needs how many units of each lot were consumed by the sale and their buy cost.
questions.schema:
BUY_LOT(lot_id NUMBER, client_id NUMBER, isin VARCHAR2(12), buy_dt DATE, qty NUMBER, price NUMBER(10,2))
-- one row per purchase; price per share in INR; same-day lots are used in lot_id order
SELL_ORDER(client_id NUMBER, isin VARCHAR2(12), sell_qty NUMBER)
-- total quantity sold per client and ISIN
questions.task: For each client and ISIN, list lot_id, buy_dt, price, qty_sold (units taken from that lot) and cost_inr (qty_sold * price), using the oldest lots first and stopping when the sold quantity is covered.
questions.hint: Compute a running SUM(qty) per client and ISIN in FIFO order; a lot is used if the quantity before it is less than sell_qty, and it gives LEAST(qty, sell_qty - quantity_before).
questions.solution:
WITH l AS (
  SELECT b.*,
         SUM(qty) OVER (PARTITION BY client_id, isin
                        ORDER BY buy_dt, lot_id
                        ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) - qty AS qty_before
  FROM   buy_lot b
)
SELECT l.client_id, l.lot_id, l.buy_dt, l.price,
       LEAST(l.qty, s.sell_qty - l.qty_before)           AS qty_sold,
       LEAST(l.qty, s.sell_qty - l.qty_before) * l.price AS cost_inr
FROM   l
JOIN   sell_order s
  ON   s.client_id = l.client_id
 AND   s.isin      = l.isin
WHERE  l.qty_before < s.sell_qty
ORDER  BY l.client_id, l.buy_dt, l.lot_id;
questions.simple: Think of a stack of biscuit packets with the oldest at the front of the cupboard. If you need 210 biscuits, you empty the oldest packets first, and from the last packet you only take what you still need. The running total tells you how many biscuits were in all the packets before this one. If that is already enough, you do not open this packet at all.
questions.remember: Running total before me decides how much I give.
questions.why: The running SUM minus the current qty gives the units in all earlier lots, so each lot can work out its own share without a loop or cursor. LEAST(qty, sell_qty - qty_before) takes the whole lot or only the remainder for the last lot touched, and the WHERE drops lots never reached. Including lot_id in the ORDER BY and using ROWS (not the default RANGE) keeps the two same-day lots from being summed together.
questions.tip: For FIFO allocation I compute the quantity before each row with a running SUM and use LEAST against the remaining demand, all in one set-based query.

questions.title: Best contact for claim updates
questions.scenario: Nandini Kulkarni runs the health claims desk and must send a claim-status message to every policyholder today. Some customers gave no mobile, some only an alternate number, some only an email, so she wants one 'best contact' per policy.
questions.schema:
POLICY_CONTACT(policy_no VARCHAR2(10), holder_name VARCHAR2(60), mobile VARCHAR2(10), alt_mobile VARCHAR2(10), email VARCHAR2(80))
-- mobile = primary number, alt_mobile = alternate number
-- any of mobile, alt_mobile, email can be NULL
questions.task: Show policy_no, holder_name and contact, where contact is the mobile if present, else alt_mobile, else email, else the text 'NO CONTACT'. Sort by policy_no.
questions.hint: COALESCE takes a list and returns the first value in it that is not NULL.
questions.solution:
SELECT policy_no,
       holder_name,
       COALESCE(mobile, alt_mobile, email, 'NO CONTACT') AS contact
FROM   policy_contact
ORDER  BY policy_no;
questions.simple: Think of calling home: first you try Papa's phone, if nobody picks up you try Mummy's phone, and if that fails you send an email. You stop at the first one that works. COALESCE does exactly this: it checks each column from left to right and gives back the first one that is not empty (NULL). If all are empty, it gives the last fallback text.
questions.remember: COALESCE = try each one, keep the first non-empty.
questions.why: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression in its list and stops evaluating as soon as it finds one (short-circuit). Unlike NVL, which takes exactly two arguments and always evaluates both, COALESCE accepts any number of arguments, all of which must be of compatible data types. Here every argument is a string, so the literal 'NO CONTACT' fits as the final default.
questions.tip: I use COALESCE instead of nested NVL calls when there are more than two fallbacks, because it reads left to right and stops at the first non-NULL value.

questions.title: RTGS payments needing one approval
questions.scenario: Rohit Agarwal in payments operations says RTGS transfers from Rs 2,00,000 up to and including Rs 5,00,000 need one checker approval, while bigger ones go to the branch head. He wants today's list for the checker queue.
questions.schema:
RTGS_TXN(utr VARCHAR2(16), sender_acct VARCHAR2(12), amount NUMBER(14,2), txn_time DATE)
-- utr = unique transaction reference
-- amount in INR
questions.task: List utr, sender_acct and amount of every RTGS payment with amount from 2,00,000 to 5,00,000 (both ends included), smallest first.
questions.hint: BETWEEN low AND high includes both the low and the high value.
questions.solution:
SELECT utr, sender_acct, amount
FROM   rtgs_txn
WHERE  amount BETWEEN 200000 AND 500000
ORDER  BY amount;
questions.simple: Imagine a ride at a fair that allows children from 120 cm to 150 cm tall. A child who is exactly 120 cm can ride, and so can one who is exactly 150 cm. BETWEEN works the same way: it keeps values inside the range and also the two edge values. So 2,00,000 and 5,00,000 are kept, but 1,99,999 and 5,00,001 are not.
questions.remember: BETWEEN includes both ends, like a ride's height limits.
questions.why: col BETWEEN a AND b is exactly col >= a AND col <= b, so both boundary values qualify. The lower value must come first: BETWEEN 500000 AND 200000 returns no rows. On DATE columns that carry a time part, BETWEEN DATE '2026-11-14' AND DATE '2026-11-14' misses rows after midnight, so date ranges are usually written as >= start AND < next day.
questions.tip: I remember that BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends, and for DATE columns with time I prefer >= start AND < end + 1 so no late-evening rows are lost.

questions.title: Second-biggest trade value per stock
questions.scenario: Aparna Desai in the broking surveillance team reviews large orders. For each stock traded on 13-11-2026 she wants the trades at the second-highest trade value, because the top value is already reviewed by an automatic rule. Two trades can have the same value.
questions.schema:
TRADE(trade_id VARCHAR2(10), symbol VARCHAR2(20), client_id VARCHAR2(10), trade_value NUMBER(14,2), trade_date DATE)
-- trade_value in INR
-- one row per executed trade
questions.task: For each symbol, return every trade whose trade_value is the second-highest distinct value for that symbol. Show symbol, trade_id, client_id and trade_value, sorted by symbol and trade_id.
questions.hint: ROW_NUMBER would call the second of two tied top trades 'number 2'; DENSE_RANK gives tied values the same rank and does not skip numbers.
questions.solution:
SELECT symbol, trade_id, client_id, trade_value
FROM  (SELECT t.*,
              DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY symbol
                                 ORDER BY trade_value DESC) AS rnk
       FROM   trade t)
WHERE  rnk = 2
ORDER  BY symbol, trade_id;
questions.simple: Think of a race where two children finish together in first place. With DENSE_RANK both get gold, and the next child gets silver, not bronze. For INFY the two 8,50,000 trades share rank 1, so 6,20,000 is the true second-highest value. For HDFCBANK the two 7,30,000 trades are both second, so both are shown.
questions.remember: DENSE_RANK: ties share a place, no places skipped.
questions.why: DENSE_RANK assigns the same rank to equal values within each PARTITION BY group and continues with the next consecutive number, so rank 2 always means the second distinct value. ROW_NUMBER would wrongly return T902 for INFY and only one of the tied HDFCBANK trades, while RANK would skip rank 2 entirely for INFY (1, 1, 3). The analytic function cannot be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE clause, so it is computed in an inline view first.
questions.tip: For 'Nth highest value' questions I use DENSE_RANK, because ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily and RANK leaves gaps after ties.
questions.output_note: INFY has two trades tied at 8,50,000 (rank 1), so its rank 2 is 6,20,000. HDFCBANK has two trades tied at rank 2.

questions.title: One-line KYC document summary
questions.scenario: Harish Patil in the KYC operations team prepares a re-KYC follow-up sheet. He wants one row per customer with the document types already received, written in a single comma-separated cell. Some customers re-uploaded the same document and some uploaded nothing.
questions.schema:
CUSTOMER(cust_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_name VARCHAR2(60))
KYC_DOC(doc_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_id VARCHAR2(10), doc_type VARCHAR2(20), uploaded_on DATE)
-- one row per upload; the same doc_type can be uploaded twice
questions.task: Show cust_id, cust_name and docs, where docs lists each distinct doc_type once in alphabetical order separated by ', '. Customers with no documents must still appear with docs = 'NONE'.
questions.hint: LEFT JOIN keeps customers with no uploads, LISTAGG(DISTINCT ...) removes repeats, and NVL turns the empty list into 'NONE'.
questions.solution:
SELECT c.cust_id,
       c.cust_name,
       NVL(LISTAGG(DISTINCT k.doc_type, ', ')
             WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY k.doc_type), 'NONE') AS docs
FROM   customer c
LEFT   JOIN kyc_doc k ON k.cust_id = c.cust_id
GROUP  BY c.cust_id, c.cust_name
ORDER  BY c.cust_id;
questions.simple: Think of writing your shopping bill on one line: 'milk, bread, eggs' instead of one item per line. If you bought bread twice, you still write bread only once. LISTAGG glues many rows into one text line, and DISTINCT makes sure each document name appears only once. A customer with nothing uploaded gets 'NONE' so they are not forgotten.
questions.remember: LISTAGG = many rows glued into one line.
questions.why: LISTAGG is an aggregate that concatenates values per group in the order given by WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...); the DISTINCT option is available from Oracle 19c. NULL values are skipped, so the LEFT JOIN row for K104 produces a NULL list, which NVL replaces. The result is VARCHAR2 and raises ORA-01489 if it exceeds the maximum length, unless ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE is used.
questions.tip: On 19c I use LISTAGG(DISTINCT col, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col), and I mention ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE for long lists to avoid ORA-01489.
questions.output_note: K101 uploaded PAN twice but it is listed once. K104 has no uploads, so the LEFT JOIN gives NULL and NVL shows NONE.

questions.title: Post EMIs, roll back only bounces
questions.scenario: Sanjay Mehra owns the nightly EMI auto-debit job. Each EMI debits the savings account and writes a loan receipt; if the account would go negative, only that EMI must be undone and marked BOUNCED, while the other EMIs in the same run stay posted.
questions.schema:
ACCT_BALANCE(acct_no VARCHAR2(10) PRIMARY KEY, balance NUMBER(14,2))
-- savings balance in INR
EMI_DUE(loan_no VARCHAR2(10), acct_no VARCHAR2(10), emi_amt NUMBER(12,2))
-- EMIs due tonight
LOAN_RECEIPT(loan_no VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- empty before the run
EMI_RUN_LOG(loan_no VARCHAR2(10), acct_no VARCHAR2(10), status VARCHAR2(10), bal_after NUMBER(14,2))
-- empty before the run
questions.task: Write an anonymous block that processes EMI_DUE in loan_no order: debit the account, insert the receipt, and if the new balance is below zero roll back just that EMI with a SAVEPOINT. Log every EMI as PAID or BOUNCED with the account balance after it, and commit once at the end.
questions.hint: Set the SAVEPOINT at the top of each loop pass, use RETURNING to read the new balance, and write the log row after any ROLLBACK TO so the log is not undone.
questions.simple: Think of playing a video game that saves a checkpoint before each level. If you lose a level, you go back to that checkpoint, not to the very start of the game. SAVEPOINT is the checkpoint before each EMI. When an EMI would make the balance go below zero, ROLLBACK TO undoes only that EMI, and all the EMIs already paid stay paid.
questions.remember: SAVEPOINT = checkpoint; ROLLBACK TO = undo only since it.
questions.why: ROLLBACK TO savepoint undoes only the changes made after that savepoint and keeps the transaction open, whereas a plain ROLLBACK would also undo every EMI posted earlier in the run. Re-using the same savepoint name in each iteration simply moves the marker forward. The log insert is placed after the ROLLBACK TO so it survives, and the single COMMIT at the end makes the whole batch atomic.
questions.tip: When one bad record must not undo a whole batch, I set a SAVEPOINT per record and ROLLBACK TO it, and I commit once at the end rather than inside the loop.
questions.output_note: EMI_RUN_LOG after the block. L2 and L4 were rolled back, so ACCT_BALANCE ends as SB101 35000, SB102 12000, SB103 0, and LOAN_RECEIPT holds only L1, L3 and L5. L5 takes SB103 to exactly 0, which is not below zero, so it is PAID.

questions.title: Card spend with every subtotal
questions.scenario: Priya Venkatesh in the cards MIS team sends a daily spend summary to the card business head. He wants totals for every card type and channel pair, plus totals per card type, per channel and a grand total, all in one result.
questions.schema:
CARD_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), card_type VARCHAR2(10), channel VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- card_type: CREDIT or DEBIT
-- channel: POS, ECOM or ATM; amount in INR
questions.task: Return card_type, channel, total_amt and txn_cnt for every combination, every card type total, every channel total and the grand total. Show 'ALL' where a column is rolled up, and order detail rows first, then card type totals, then channel totals, then the grand total.
questions.hint: CUBE(a, b) produces all four grouping levels; GROUPING(col) returns 1 on rows where that column was rolled up.
questions.solution:
SELECT DECODE(GROUPING(card_type), 1, 'ALL', card_type) AS card_type,
       DECODE(GROUPING(channel),   1, 'ALL', channel)   AS channel,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amt,
       COUNT(*)    AS txn_cnt
FROM   card_txn
GROUP  BY CUBE(card_type, channel)
ORDER  BY GROUPING_ID(card_type, channel), card_type, channel;
questions.simple: Think of a class marks sheet where you add up marks for each child, for each subject, and then the total of everything. CUBE does all these totals in one go. It gives the total for each card type with each channel, then each card type alone, then each channel alone, and finally one grand total. 'ALL' shows which column was added up.
questions.remember: CUBE = every possible subtotal, plus the grand total.
questions.why: GROUP BY CUBE(a, b) is shorthand for GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), (b), ()), so it returns 2^n grouping levels for n columns, unlike ROLLUP which only produces the hierarchical levels (a, b), (a), (). GROUPING(col) distinguishes a subtotal NULL from a real NULL value in the data. GROUPING_ID(card_type, channel) packs those bits into one number (0, 1, 2, 3), which is handy for ordering or filtering levels.
questions.tip: I explain that ROLLUP gives hierarchical subtotals while CUBE gives every combination, and I use GROUPING or GROUPING_ID rather than NVL to label the subtotal rows.
questions.output_note: CREDIT has no ATM rows and DEBIT has one row per channel, so only 5 detail rows exist. Grand total is 85,000 over 6 transactions.

questions.title: Apply FD renewals, closures and openings
questions.scenario: Kiran Bhosale runs the fixed deposit maturity batch on 14-11-2026. The day's event file renews some FDs with interest added, closes others that are paid out, and opens new ones; closed FDs must disappear from FD_ACTIVE and an unknown closure must be ignored. He wants it in one MERGE statement.
questions.schema:
FD_ACTIVE(fd_no VARCHAR2(10) PRIMARY KEY, cust_name VARCHAR2(60), principal NUMBER(14,2), maturity_date DATE)
-- live fixed deposits, principal in INR
FD_EVENT(fd_no VARCHAR2(10), cust_name VARCHAR2(60), event_type VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(14,2), new_maturity DATE)
-- event_type: RENEW (new principal and maturity), CLOSE (paid out), OPEN (new FD)
questions.task: Write one MERGE that updates principal and maturity_date for RENEW events, deletes the FD for CLOSE events, and inserts OPEN events that are not yet in FD_ACTIVE. A CLOSE for an FD not in FD_ACTIVE must not be inserted.
questions.hint: A MERGE update branch can end with DELETE WHERE, which removes only rows that the update just touched; add a WHERE to the INSERT branch too.
questions.solution:
MERGE INTO fd_active t
USING fd_event s
ON (t.fd_no = s.fd_no)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET t.principal     = s.amount,
             t.maturity_date = s.new_maturity
  DELETE WHERE s.event_type = 'CLOSE'
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (fd_no, cust_name, principal, maturity_date)
  VALUES (s.fd_no, s.cust_name, s.amount, s.new_maturity)
  WHERE s.event_type = 'OPEN';
questions.simple: Think of a class register on the first day of term. Children who are staying get their new class written in, children who left the school are struck off, and new children are added at the bottom. MERGE does all three jobs in one pass. Its DELETE part only strikes off rows it has just updated, and the INSERT has its own rule so only real new FDs are added.
questions.remember: MERGE: update, strike off, add new, in one pass.
questions.why: In Oracle the DELETE WHERE clause belongs to the WHEN MATCHED branch, so it can only remove rows that were matched and updated in this MERGE; it is evaluated after the update. Source columns such as s.event_type can be referenced there, and the optional WHERE on WHEN NOT MATCHED stops the unknown FD099 closure from being inserted. Each target row may be matched by at most one source row, otherwise MERGE raises ORA-30926.
questions.tip: I mention that MERGE's DELETE WHERE only affects rows updated by that same MERGE, and that duplicate source keys cause ORA-30926, so I de-duplicate the source first.
questions.output_note: FD_ACTIVE after the MERGE. FD102 was updated then deleted, FD103 had no event and is unchanged, FD105 was inserted, and FD099 was ignored.

questions.title: Find missing GL voucher number ranges
questions.scenario: CA Ritu Goel, the concurrent auditor, must report any break in the voucher number series at each branch, because a missing voucher can hide a deleted or unauthorised entry. She wants each missing range once, not one row per missing number.
questions.schema:
GL_VOUCHER(branch_code VARCHAR2(5), voucher_no NUMBER(8), voucher_date DATE, amount NUMBER(14,2))
-- voucher_no is meant to be continuous within each branch
-- amount in INR
questions.task: For each branch, list every missing range of voucher numbers as gap_from, gap_to and missing_cnt, sorted by branch_code and gap_from.
questions.hint: Use LEAD to put the next voucher number beside each row; a jump of more than 1 means numbers are missing in between.
questions.solution:
SELECT branch_code,
       voucher_no + 1             AS gap_from,
       next_no - 1                AS gap_to,
       next_no - voucher_no - 1   AS missing_cnt
FROM  (SELECT branch_code, voucher_no,
              LEAD(voucher_no) OVER (PARTITION BY branch_code
                                     ORDER BY voucher_no) AS next_no
       FROM   gl_voucher)
WHERE  next_no - voucher_no > 1
ORDER  BY branch_code, gap_from;
questions.simple: Think of the numbered pages of your notebook. If page 2 is followed by page 5, you know pages 3 and 4 were torn out. LEAD lets each row peek at the next voucher number. If the next number is more than one bigger, the numbers in between are missing, and we print that range once.
questions.remember: LEAD peeks ahead; a jump bigger than 1 is a gap.
questions.why: LEAD(voucher_no) OVER (PARTITION BY branch_code ORDER BY voucher_no) returns the next number in the same branch, so a difference greater than 1 marks a gap of next - current - 1 numbers. The last voucher of each branch has a NULL LEAD, and NULL - n > 1 is not true, so it drops out without extra code. This reports ranges in a single pass instead of generating every possible number with CONNECT BY and using MINUS.
questions.tip: To find gaps I compare each row with LEAD of the ordered key and report next - current > 1, which gives ranges in one scan instead of generating all numbers.
questions.output_note: B01 is missing 1003-1004 and 1006-1008; B02 is missing 2003.

lessons.why: LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row's value unless you widen the window, a common bug in month-end and closing-rate reports.
lessons.explain: When an analytic function has ORDER BY but no frame, Oracle uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. For SUM that gives a running total, but for LAST_VALUE it means the last row seen so far is the current row, so you get the row's own value back. To get the true last value of the partition, state ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or use FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY ... DESC. Adding IGNORE NULLS turns it into a carry-forward tool.
lessons.example:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-02' d, 83.10 rate FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-03', 83.25 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-04', 83.18 FROM dual
)
SELECT d, rate,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS default_frame,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS closing_rate
FROM r;
-- default_frame: 83.10, 83.25, 83.18   closing_rate: 83.18, 83.18, 83.18
lessons.gotcha: LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) looks right in a quick test but just echoes x on every row.
lessons.line: For a closing value per period I use LAST_VALUE with an explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame, or FIRST_VALUE ordered descending, because the default frame stops at the current row.
lessons.simple: LAST_VALUE sounds like 'give me the last one', but by default it only looks from the top down to the current row, so the last one it sees is itself. To see the real last row, tell it to look all the way to the end.
lessons.remember: Tell LAST_VALUE to look to the end: UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

lessons.why: Top-N queries written with ROWNUM in the same SELECT as ORDER BY return the wrong rows, a classic interview trap and a real reporting bug.
lessons.simple: Imagine a teacher who hands out medals to the first 2 children who walk in, and only after that lines them up by height. The medal winners were never the tallest, just the first through the door. ROWNUM is that door number: Oracle gives it out before ORDER BY sorts. So sort first in an inner query, then hand out the numbers.
lessons.remember: ROWNUM is given before sorting; sort inside, filter outside.
lessons.explain: ROWNUM is assigned to each row as it passes the WHERE clause, before ORDER BY runs, so WHERE ROWNUM <= 2 ... ORDER BY bal DESC picks any two rows and then sorts just those. The fix is to sort in an inline view and apply ROWNUM outside it, or in 12c and later use ORDER BY ... FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY (or ROW_NUMBER() OVER for top-N per group). WHERE ROWNUM > 1 never returns anything, because the first row fails, so the next row becomes ROWNUM 1 again. FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES also keeps rows tied with the last one.
lessons.gotcha: SELECT ... WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY amount DESC returns five random rows sorted, not the top five.
lessons.line: Because ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY, I either sort in an inline view and filter ROWNUM outside, or simply use FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY.

lessons.why: Picking the wrong ranking function on tied values is one of the most common interview traps in top-N and Nth-highest questions.
lessons.simple: Think of a race where two runners cross the line together. ROW_NUMBER is the strict referee who still gives them 1 and 2. RANK gives both of them 1 and the next runner 3, skipping 2. DENSE_RANK gives both of them 1 and the next runner 2, without skipping. All three just put numbers on rows in the order you ask for.
lessons.remember: ROW_NUMBER unique, RANK skips, DENSE_RANK never skips.
lessons.explain: All three are analytic functions that need OVER (ORDER BY ...) and can restart per group with PARTITION BY. ROW_NUMBER always gives 1, 2, 3 even on ties, so which tied row gets the lower number is not deterministic unless you add a tie-breaker column. RANK gives tied rows the same number and then jumps (1, 1, 3), while DENSE_RANK gives the same number and continues (1, 1, 2). Use ROW_NUMBER for de-duplication or exactly-N rows, RANK for 'positions' like a competition, and DENSE_RANK for 'Nth highest distinct value'.
lessons.example:
WITH b AS (
  SELECT 'Arun' cust, 90000 bal FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Bina', 90000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Chetan', 70000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Divya', 50000 FROM dual
)
SELECT cust, bal,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC, cust) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC)       AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC)       AS drnk
FROM   b;
-- Arun 90000 1 1 1 | Bina 90000 2 1 1 | Chetan 70000 3 3 2 | Divya 50000 4 4 3
lessons.gotcha: Using ROW_NUMBER = 1 to find 'the top customer' silently drops a customer who is tied for first place.
lessons.line: I pick ROW_NUMBER when I need exactly one row per group, RANK when ties should share a position with gaps, and DENSE_RANK for Nth-highest distinct values.
